opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think about this a lot, because I've been in robotics for over forty years now, and I've seen a few of these cycles come and go. The Gartner hype cycle is a really useful frame: a new technology triggers enormous excitement, expectations climb to a "peak of inflated expectations," and then, when reality doesn't keep pace, you fall into what they call the "trough of disillusionment." Eventually, if the technology is real, you climb back up the "slope of enlightenment" to a plateau of actual productivity.

Right now, I'd say robotics, and humanoids in particular, are right at or near that peak. There are billions of dollars flowing in. You see these beautiful videos of robots doing backflips, dancing, folding laundry. And people extrapolate. They've just watched large language models seem to come out of nowhere and do things nobody expected, so they assume the same thing is about to happen with robots: that in a year or two, we'll have a robot in every home doing the dishes.

My concern is that that's not going to happen on that timeline, and the gap between expectation and reality is going to cause real damage.

Part of the reason is what I call the data gap. Language models were trained on essentially the whole internet, which is the equivalent of something like a hundred thousand years of human reading. For robots, we don't have anything close to that. There's no internet of robot motion data, of how it actually feels to grasp a slippery glass or pick up a crumpled shirt. People are trying to collect it through teleoperation and simulation, and that's valuable, but we're orders of magnitude away. And this is really Moravec's paradox again: the things that are easy for us, like picking up an object you've never seen, are extraordinarily hard for machines, while the things that seem hard, like chess, turned out to be relatively easy.

Also, a lot of those videos are, let's say, carefully curated. Sometimes they're teleoperated, sometimes sped up, sometimes they're the one successful take out of many. That's not dishonest exactly, but it creates a distorted impression.

So the danger of the bubble bursting is this: if investors and the public expect general-purpose home robots in two years, and that doesn't materialize, there could be a backlash. Funding dries up. Startups fold. Talented students leave the field. We've seen this before with AI winters. And that would be a real shame, because there is genuine, exciting progress happening. It's just more incremental than the hype suggests.

What I'd like to see is a more measured approach, being honest about what robots can and can't do, focusing on applications where they really can add value right now, like logistics, sorting packages in warehouses, certain kinds of manufacturing, and building up from there. I often say I'm an optimist about robotics in the long run, but a skeptic about the short-term timelines. If we can manage expectations, I think we can avoid a deep trough and keep steady progress going.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes backlash and damage if robots do not meet expectations, but does not say people may dismiss the entire field as having no substance.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says that if expectations are unmet, there could be a backlash and “Funding dries up.”

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the Gartner hype cycle is this very simple curve that I think is actually quite insightful. You have a technology trigger, and then expectations shoot up to what they call the peak of inflated expectations. And then there's a crash — the trough of disillusionment — and then, if the technology is real, you eventually climb what they call the slope of enlightenment to a plateau of productivity.

What worries me about robotics right now is that we're very close to that peak. You've got humanoid robots in every other video on social media, you've got people saying we're a year or two away from robots doing your laundry and your dishes and working in every factory. And a lot of that is teleoperated, or it's cherry-picked, or it's running in a very carefully staged environment. The public doesn't see that. Investors often don't see that either.

The reason I think the bursting is dangerous — rather than just a correction — is that we've been here before. I lived through what people call the "AI winters," and there was a kind of robotics winter too. When expectations get too far ahead of what the systems can actually do, there's a backlash. Funding dries up, students stop going into the field, companies fold, and some of the genuinely good work gets thrown out along with the hype. It sets things back years. And it's not that the underlying technology was bad — it's that it was oversold.

So I'm not a pessimist about robotics. I'm actually very optimistic about the long term. But I think the people in the field have a responsibility to be honest about where we are. What I try to say is: there's been real progress, especially in grasping and manipulation with the new learning methods, but the gap between a demo and a reliable system that works in your home, in the rain, with a kid running around, is enormous. If we're clear about that, I think we can get through the trough with less damage. If we keep promising the moon, the fall is going to be harder.

r001.rationale: The response says backlash can cause good work to be thrown out with the hype, but does not say people dismiss the entire field as having no substance.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says that when expectations outrun systems’ capabilities, “funding dries up.”

astra-6.text:
I think the danger is that expectations get so far ahead of what the technology can actually do that people lose confidence in the whole field. In the Gartner hype cycle, you have this peak of inflated expectations, and then you fall into the trough of disillusionment. Robotics is particularly vulnerable because a compelling demonstration can make a robot look much more capable than it really is. You see it succeed once, but you don’t necessarily see the failures or how carefully the environment was set up.

And the gap between a demonstration and something that works reliably every day is enormous. If people invest on the assumption that we’ve already crossed that gap, they’re going to be disappointed. Funding can dry up, and useful research can get caught in that reaction.

So I think we have a responsibility to be enthusiastic but also very clear about the limitations. What conditions does the robot work under? How often does it fail? How much human assistance does it need? There’s real progress to be excited about. We don’t need to promise that robots will be able to do everything in order to make that progress valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says people may lose confidence in the whole field, but does not say they will dismiss it as having no substance.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says funding can dry up after people are disappointed by unmet expectations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the danger is that expectations get so far ahead of what the technology can actually deliver that people lose confidence in the whole field. In the Gartner hype cycle, you have this peak of inflated expectations, followed by the trough of disillusionment. And robotics is particularly vulnerable because a compelling demonstration can make a problem look solved, even though getting that same system to work reliably, day after day, is tremendously difficult.

That doesn’t mean the progress isn’t real. But if investors and customers expect general-purpose robots to arrive immediately, they’re going to be disappointed. Then funding can dry up, including for people doing very solid work.

So I think we have a responsibility to communicate both the advances and the limitations. What can the robot do? Under what conditions? How often does it fail? Those questions are less exciting than a spectacular video, but they’re what let us build applications that are actually useful—and sustain confidence over time.

r001.rationale: The response says people may lose confidence in the whole field, but does not state that they may dismiss it as having no substance.

r002.rationale: It says disappointment can cause funding to dry up, including funding for solid work in robotics.
